101.title: Clean-room ProPicks India — Rebuilding the Four-Pillar Score From Public Sources
101.subtitle: A from-scratch reconstruction of thefactor structurebehind Investing.com's ProPicks India strategies, inferred purely from their public methodology page and the press releases they publish on every monthly rebalance. Nothing was taken from the product — no paywall bypassed, no private endpoint called, no proprietary code or model weights obtained. It is then tested on Indian small-caps and mid-caps to ask the only question that matters: does that structure actually earn anything?

pills.text: four-pillar composite beats its index — but the edge is front-loaded
~4.5 names rotated/month, matching their stated 4–8

paragraphs: Over 40 monthly rebalances the four-pillar composite returned +29.4% CAGR on small-caps against +16.6% for the NIFTY Smallcap 250, and +32.5% on mid-caps against +15.8% for the NIFTY Midcap 150 — after real statutory and brokerage charges on a full monthly re-slice of the book. Plain momentum, the control, lands at +21.0% and +25.8%. Adding value, growth and quality on top of momentum is worth real money in both universes over the full window.

The caveat is the second half of the window, and it is the part to actually trade on. Cut the period in half and small-cap outperformance falls from +26.0pp of CAGR to +1.3pp, where plain momentum beats the composite outright. Mid-caps hold up far better. The structure works; the 30%-a-year headline does not survive scrutiny, and on top of that every reconstruction here carries survivorship bias that flatters all variants equally. See the robustness table and limitations below.

panels.heading: What was reconstructed, and how

pills.text: public sources only — no paywall, no private endpoints

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the inference chain from their published material to the scoring rules actually tested here. The full write-up is in docs/propicks-india-recon.md.
paragraphs: The invariant four-bullet structure across every published rationale is the tell. It is a momentum + value-vs-fair-value + growth + quality composite, ranked monthly, with a fair-value gate.

The mechanism is specific and worth naming: buy earnings acceleration before the multiple re-rates, and rotate out once it has. That is why a rationale can say "+47% in three months" and "trades at just 11x, PEG 0.19" in the same sentence — price rose while earnings rose faster, so the multiple compressed. This report tests whether that structure earns anything when rebuilt from scratch.
list_items: Rebalance on thefirst trading dayof each month, at that session's close.
15–20slots,equal weight,4–8names rotated per month.
Removal is arank push-out, explicitly not a sell signal.

Every add/remove ships a rationale citing four things: a 3/6/12-month price return, a P/E and P/B with a "fair value" and its % upside, a revenue/EBITDA/profit growth rate, and the balance-sheet state.
Universe filters first: market-cap band, index membership, liquidity floor, no penny stocks.

panels.heading: What trading this actually costs
panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — a full equal-weight re-slice every month touches the whole book, which is why the gap between the loaded and frictionless rows is wide. The real strategy only rotates 4–8 of its 20 names, so this is deliberately pessimistic.
paragraphs: Cost drag over the window is 7.23pp of CAGR on small-caps and 7.41pp on mid-caps. Implied rotation is 4.5 and 4.2 names per month respectively — which lands inside the 4–8 band they state publicly, a small but real confirmation that the reconstructed turnover is in the right neighbourhood. Implementing it their way (trade only the 4–8 changes, never re-slice the retained names) would recover roughly half the cost drag shown here.

panels.heading: Limitations — read before trusting any number above

pills.text: mandatory, not decorative

list_items: Survivorship bias is the big one.Today's NIFTY Smallcap 250 / Midcap 150 constituent lists are applied retroactively to every rebalance. Stocks that fell out of the index, delisted, merged or went bankrupt are missing from the entire history. This flatters every variant on this page and it is strongest for smallcaps, whose membership churns most. No result here should be read as a live-tradable track record.

The window is short and was kind.40 rebalances over 3.3 years, mid-2023 onward — a period in which the benchmark itself compounded at 16.6% (smallcap) and 15.8% (midcap). The half-window table above is the antidote; use it, not the headline.

The fair-value gate is a stand-in, not a replica.Their fair-value engine is proprietary and unrecoverable. An absolute anchor was tried first and fails outright on Indian smallcaps: a Graham number puts the median stock 54–82%belowfair value, so only 4–24% of names would ever clear such a gate. What is used instead is a peer-relative anchor (the universe's median P/E and median P/B applied to each stock's own earnings and book) — no invented macro assumption, but it is a proxy for 'cheaper than the median peer'.

The 90-day reporting lag.A fundamental period is only usable 90 days after its period-end. Indian annual results for a March year-end are due within roughly 60 days, so this is deliberately conservative — it costs staleness rather than risking look-ahead. Without it, every value/growth/quality reading would be look-ahead and the whole result would be a fiction.

Only ~4–5 annual periods are availablefrom the data source, so the four-pillar variants cannot start before mid-2023 once the lag and a prior-year growth base are both satisfied. That is the entire reason for the short window.

Full equal-weight re-slice every month.That charges buy and sell costs on ~100% of the book each rebalance. The real strategy rotates only 4–8 of 20 names, so these cost-loaded figures are aconservative upper boundon cost drag — the frictionless rows show how much. No impact cost, no taxes, no slippage beyond the sourced statutory ladder.

Growth is measured off each company's own fiscal calendar.A stock's 'prior year' is its previous annual period in the data, not a calendar-aligned fiscal year — non-March year-ends are measured on their own clock rather than silently re-aligned.

Unadjusted prices, no dividends modelled, no intraday fills, and signal-at-close / fill-at-close on the rebalance day (matching how the real strategy states it rebalances at the end of the first session).

panels.heading: The rule, and the honest result up front

pills.text: reduces drawdown vs. pure momentum
underperforms just leaving it alone
5 trigger cycles in 17.6 years

paragraphs: Start 50% Midcap150 Momentum-10 / 50% gold. The moment the momentum leg falls 20% below its OWN running peak, sell 100% of the gold and put it all into momentum — an all-in lump sum funded by the diversification cushion. Stay 100% momentum until it makes a brand-new all-time high (fully recovers), then reset to exactly 50/50 and repeat. This happened 5 times over 2009-01-02–2026-08-24, averaging 237 days to recover each time.

The catch does what it's designed to do on the risk side — shallower drawdown than holding pure momentum alone. But on return, it underperforms simply buying 50/50 once and never touching it again (+31.2% CAGR vs. +35.3%) — and it even underperforms a plain CALENDAR-rebalanced 50/50 blend on drawdown (-29.2% vs. -21.7%). Repeatedly resetting back to 50/50 after each recovery turns out to cap the compounding of the far-faster-growing momentum leg more than the "buy the dip" timing helps — see the honesty note below for the mechanism.

panels.heading: Why "buying the dip" here still lost to doing nothing

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Over 2009-01-02–2026-08-24, momentum alone compounded at +40.5% a year versus gold's +13.9% — momentum grew roughly 403x versus gold's 9x over the full window. A 50/50 split that is NEVER rebalanced naturally drifts to be almost entirely momentum within a few years, simply because the faster-compounding asset dominates the mix — that drift is exactly what "static, never touched" is capturing, and it's a large share of why it wins.

The catch rule does the opposite at every single cycle: the moment momentum recovers from a dip, it forcibly resets the mix back to 50/50 — selling down exactly the asset that was about to keep compounding fastest, and buying back into gold, right as momentum turns UP again. Each of the 5 reset points is a small, repeated tax on the momentum leg's own compounding, paid in exchange for a real but partial reduction in how deep the worst drawdown gets.

That trade-off shows up exactly as expected: the catch's max drawdown (-29.2%) is shallower than pure momentum's (-35.1%) — the rule does work as risk management. It just isn't a free lunch: plain periodic rebalancing, with no drawdown-timing logic at all, achieves an even shallower drawdown (-21.7%) for a similar return give-up, suggesting the discipline of rebalancing itself — not the specific -20%/new-high timing rule — is doing most of the risk reduction here.

25.title: Midcap Momentum 10 — Every Semi-Annual Rebalance Offset, Compared
25.subtitle: The exact same strategy, only the calendar shifts: Jan/Jul, Feb/Aug, Mar/Sep, Apr/Oct, May/Nov, and the "normal" Jun/Dec used everywhere else in this project — same universe, same top-10/equal-weight/6m-12m-momentum formula, same 2008-2026 window.

panels.heading: The question, and the honest result up front

pills.text: 5.1pp CAGR spread across all 6 offsets
the "normal" Jun/Dec offset is mid-pack, not best or worst

paragraphs: Every report in this project that uses Midcap150 Momentum 10 checks momentum, and rebalances, every June and December — a convention borrowed from the real NIFTY200 Momentum index's own schedule, not something specifically chosen because it works best for THIS strategy. Since momentum is measured 6 and 12 months back from the rebalance date, moving that date to a different month pair genuinely changes which stocks get picked at every single rebalance, not just when the reshuffle happens.

Across all six possible offsets, CAGR ranges from +38.4% (Mar/Sep) to +43.6% (Apr/Oct) — a 5.1 percentage-point spread — while max drawdown ranges from -29.5% (May/Nov) to -39.5% (Apr/Oct). The "normal" Jun/Dec offset this project has used all along (+40.6% / -35.1%) lands squarely in the middle of that range on both dimensions — not the best case, not the worst, which is the honest, reassuring reading: the strategy's edge doesn't appear to hinge on having picked a lucky rebalance month.

panels.heading: Why the offset matters less than you might expect

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Each offset checks the same 6-month/12-month risk-adjusted momentum formula on 36 different dates spread 6 months apart across the same 18-year history — different SPECIFIC dates, but similar SEASONAL coverage: over 18 years, every offset ends up rebalancing through roughly the same mix of bull runs, corrections, and recoveries, just measured from a different monthly starting point each time. That's the statistical reason the six results cluster in a relatively narrow 5.1-point CAGR band rather than diverging wildly — the underlying momentum signal in Indian midcaps over this period was real and persistent enough to show up regardless of which specific month it's sampled from.

That said, 5.1 percentage points of CAGR compounded over 18 years is NOT a trivial difference in final wealth — it is the gap between Apr/Oct's +62,703.4% and Mar/Sep's +33,621.5% net return over the identical window. Some of that gap is likely genuine (certain months may happen to catch momentum inflection points slightly earlier or later than others), and some of it is noise from a single 18-year historical path — with only 36 rebalances per offset, this is not a large enough sample to say with confidence that Apr/Oct is a permanently better calendar choice, only that it happened to be over this specific history.

The practical takeaway: the "normal" Jun/Dec convention this project has used throughout was a reasonable, defensible choice (it borrows the real NIFTY200 Momentum index's actual schedule) — and this report confirms it was not an accidentally-lucky or accidentally-unlucky pick relative to the five alternatives, landing near the middle of the pack on both return and drawdown.

27.title: Midcap Momentum 10 — Stop-Loss Overlay: 15% vs. 30%, vs. the Original
27.subtitle: Same exact selection/weighting as reports 11-19, 24, 25 — but the moment a position falls a fixed % below its own entry price, it's exited immediately instead of waiting for the next June/December rebalance. Tested at two thresholds.

pills.text: 15%: 43.3% of positions stopped out
30%: 12.5% of positions stopped out
a looser stop hurts less, but neither beats the original

paragraphs: Everything about the strategy stays identical — same top-10 selection by 6m/12m risk-adjusted momentum, same equal weighting, same June/December rebalance — except each position is now watched every trading day, and exited the moment it touches a fixed % below its entry price (checked via intraday LOW, filled realistically at the day's open if it gapped through — same methodology as report 22's RSI rotation). Widening the stop from 15% to 30% cuts the CAGR damage roughly in half.

Original (no stop): +40.6% CAGR / -35.1% DD. 15% stop: +23.6% CAGR / -32.5% DD — 43.3% of all positions stopped out. 30% stop: +35.0% CAGR / -32.1% DD — only 12.5% stopped out. The looser 30% stop gives up much less return (5.6% points vs. 15%'s 17.0% points) for a very similar drawdown improvement — see the honesty note below.

panels.heading: Why the looser 30% stop is the better trade-off

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Midcap momentum picks are, by construction, already-volatile stocks that just had a strong 6-12 month run — the kind of names that can easily give back 15% in an ordinary pullback WITHOUT the underlying trend actually being over. A 15% stop on a 6-month holding period is tight enough to get triggered by routine volatility, which is why 43.3% of all 360 positions taken over 18 years ended up stopped out at 15% — versus only 12.5% at 30%, where the stop is wide enough to mostly let ordinary swings play out and only fire on genuinely severe breakdowns.

That difference shows up directly in what each threshold gives up: positions stopped out at 15% averaged -15.3% versus the 198 that rode to rebalance averaging +34.9% — a huge gap between what got cut short and what the strategy's real edge lives in. At 30%, far fewer positions (45 vs. 156) get caught in that trade-off, which is exactly why 30%'s CAGR (+35.0%) sits so much closer to the original's (+40.6%) than 15%'s does (+23.6%).

Yet both thresholds land in almost the same place on drawdown (-32.5% vs. -32.1%) — meaning the EXTRA tail-risk protection the tighter 15% stop is supposedly buying, over and above what 30% already provides, turns out to be worth very little. For this specific strategy, a looser stop (or arguably no stop at all, per the original report 27 finding) is the better risk/reward trade-off than a tight one.

paragraphs: Halving the portfolio from 10 stocks to 5, with no other change to the selection formula or rebalance schedule, is a direct test of whether concentrating a momentum bet into fewer, higher-conviction names pays off. Over 2008-12-31–2026-08-21, Momentum-5 compounded at +33.1% versus Momentum-10's +30.7% — a real, meaningful edge from concentration.

That edge is not free: Momentum-5's max drawdown (-39.1%) is deeper than Momentum-10's (-35.3%), and it spent longer underwater (909 days vs. 693 days) — exactly what basic diversification math predicts: fewer positions means each one's idiosyncratic move (good or bad) has twice the impact on the whole portfolio.

panels.heading: Why concentration cuts both ways

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Both portfolios use the identical formula to rank the same 100 stocks — Momentum-5 simply keeps only the top half of what Momentum-10 would have held. On average, whatever made those top 5 rank above positions 6-10 continued to be true often enough over 18 years for the extra concentration to pay off (2.4% points of extra CAGR). But that same logic means Momentum-5 has no cushion at all if even ONE of its 5 picks turns out to be a momentum trap (a stock whose recent strength was about to reverse) — a single bad pick is 20% of the book, versus 10% in the 10-stock version.

That's exactly the trade-off visible in the numbers: better average return, worse worst-case, and a longer stretch spent recovering from that worst case (909 days vs. 693 days). Neither number is "wrong" — this is the standard concentration-vs-diversification trade-off showing up in a real backtest, not a flaw in either construction.

30.title: Midcap Momentum 10 — No Stop-Loss, Just a Breakeven Profit-Lock
30.subtitle: Same exact selection/weighting as reports 11-19, 24, 25, 27 — no downside stop at all. Instead: once a position has run up 30% from entry, arm a protective exit at cost — if it falls all the way back to breakeven before the next rebalance, exit immediately at 0%, rather than riding it down further or waiting.

pills.text: only 5.3% of positions ever triggered the rule
near-neutral impact — a much smaller effect than either stop-loss threshold

paragraphs: This rule only ever fires for a position that BOTH ran up 30%+ from entry AND later gave essentially all of that gain back before the next rebalance — a much narrower trigger condition than report 27's fixed-percentage-loss stops. Over 2008-12-31–2026-08-24, that happened to just 19 of 360 positions (5.3%) — versus 15%'s 43.3% and 30%'s 12.5% of positions affected in report 27.

The result is correspondingly small: CAGR barely moves, from +40.6% (original) to +39.6% (with the lock) — a 1.0% point difference, far smaller than either of report 27's stop-loss variants — and max drawdown is essentially unchanged (-35.1% vs. -35.1%). This rule locks in exactly what it's designed to: guaranteeing a big winner can never fully round-trip back to a loss, without materially touching the strategy's overall risk/return profile.

panels.heading: Why this rule barely moves the needle

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Report 27's stop-losses fire on a SINGLE condition (price falls X% from entry) — easy to trigger, which is why 43.3% of positions got caught at a 15% stop. This rule requires TWO conditions in sequence: the position must first prove it can run up 30%, and THEN give essentially all of that entire gain back before the next rebalance. Most positions that reach +30% either keep running (never re-test entry) or pull back only partially — a full round-trip all the way to breakeven is a narrow, specific pattern, which is exactly why it only happened 19 times in 360 positions across 18 years.

What this rule DOES guarantee, on the 19 times it fired, is that a position which was once a big winner can never turn into an outright loss on the way back down — the average locked-out return was -0.3%, almost exactly breakeven by construction. Whether those specific 19 positions would have ended up positive or negative by the ACTUAL next rebalance (had the rule not intervened) isn't shown here — that counterfactual wasn't computed — but given how few positions are affected, either way the portfolio-level impact was always going to be small.

The practical takeaway: this is a genuinely different kind of rule than a stop-loss — it protects a specific outcome (never letting a confirmed winner become a loser) rather than capping downside broadly, and it costs almost nothing to add because it so rarely fires. It is not a substitute for a stop-loss if the goal is limiting how much any single position can lose — for that, report 27's 30% threshold remains the better-tested option.

31.title: Midcap150 Momentum 10 — Carried-Position Trade Log, 2015 to Date
31.subtitle: Same reconstruction as reports 24/26/27/30, but every stock's real continuous run in the top 10 is ONE row — New / Carried / Exited — instead of a fresh row at every rebalance it survives.

pills.text: 169 closed positions, 10 still open
avg 1.37 rebalances held, longest 4

paragraphs: Reports 24 and 26 showed every rebalance-to-rebalance leg as its own trade row — technically accurate to how the strategy's equity curve is computed (the whole portfolio is re-split equally across the top 10 at every rebalance), but it makes a stock that survives 3-4 rebalances running look like 3-4 separate trades. This report instead tracks each stock's real, uninterrupted tenure in the top 10 as ONE row: it opens the first time the stock is picked (NEW), stays open through every rebalance it's still selected (CARRIED — tagged, not a new row), and closes the moment it's finally dropped (EXITED), with ONE entry price, ONE exit price, and the total gain/loss across the whole run.

Over 2015-01-02–2026-08-24, that's 179 distinct positions instead of the much larger leg-count reports 24/26 would show for the same period — win rate 65.1%, average winner +71.4%, average loser -13.6%. The strategy itself is unchanged: +36.8% CAGR / -35.1% drawdown vs. the midcap ETF's +20.3% / -38.4% over the same window — only how the trade log is PRESENTED changes; see the limitations panel below for the one bookkeeping simplification this requires.

panels.heading: What merging changes, and what it doesn't

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: A stock's total price return from the day it first entered to the day it finally exited is exactly the same number whether you compute it directly (exit price ÷ entry price) or by chaining together every intermediate rebalance-to-rebalance leg — the interim prices cancel out. So every % return figure in this trade log is identical to what you'd get by carefully chaining reports 24/26's per-leg numbers for the same stock; nothing about the actual price performance changes. What changes is READABILITY: 179 rows instead of a much larger leg-count for the same 2015-to-date window, with each row telling the complete story of one holding.

The one place this report's numbers genuinely diverge from the strategy's real mechanics is DOLLAR P&L: the real strategy resets every position back to an equal 1/10th share of the total portfolio at every single rebalance (even for a stock that's continuing), so a long-running winner's dollar weight in the real portfolio doesn't just keep compounding untouched the way it does in this report's "alloc × total % return" bookkeeping. panels.heading: Why 2x leverage doesn't give you 2x the return — and why looser margin isn't automatically safer

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Ignoring costs and margin calls entirely, doubling each position's exposure would compound to roughly double the frictionless strategy's already-large multiple — arithmetically much more than "2x the CAGR" once compounded over 36 rebalances, since leverage amplifies BOTH the size of each period's gain and the base it compounds from. Real MTF eats into that in three separate ways: +0.24% + +0.22% of round-trip transaction costs on DOUBLE the notional (vs. cash), +9.69% p.a. interest on the borrowed half (averaging 4.37% of a position's own capital per ~6-month hold), and — the big one — margin calls that force-crystallize a loss at the worst possible moment instead of letting a position ride out a temporary dip.

That third effect is why the maintenance-margin ASSUMPTION matters so much, and why the relationship isn't what you'd first guess. At a 40% maintenance threshold (margin calls fire on roughly a 23.1%-37.5% range of price drops depending on the exact threshold — see the table above), 133 of 360 positions (36.9%) got force-sold — MORE than three times as often as at 20% maintenance (21 calls, 5.8%). A tighter (lower) maintenance requirement gives a volatile momentum stock more room to have an ordinary bad month WITHOUT being forced out — which is exactly why the 20% scenario ends up with the HIGHEST CAGR of the three (+59.5%) despite being the "loosest" margin rule, and the 40% scenario the lowest (+37.5%) despite being the "safest"-sounding one.

None of the three scenarios avoid a deep drawdown, though — all three land between -62.3% and -59.4%, meaningfully worse than the frictionless strategy's own -35.1%. The margin-call mechanism changes WHEN and HOW OFTEN losses get crystallized, but 2x leverage on an already-volatile momentum strategy is a deeper hole to climb out of under every assumption tested here.

34.title: Midcap Momentum 10 — Relative Momentum (Excess Return over NIFTY 50)
34.subtitle: Same top-10, equal-weight, June/December strategy — but ranked on EXCESS return over NIFTY 50 (stock's 6m/12m return minus NIFTY 50's own 6m/12m return over the identical window) instead of the original's absolute return. paragraphs: Subtracting NIFTY 50's own return from every stock's return before ranking shifts every stock's number by the SAME amount that day — which, on its own, wouldn't change the ranking at all (subtracting a constant preserves rank order). What actually changes the outcome is that this shift happens BEFORE dividing by each stock's own (different) volatility — so the same constant shift affects a low-volatility stock's ratio more than a high-volatility stock's. That's a real mechanism, just a much gentler one than report 33's skip-month change, which is exactly why the overlap here (92.2%) is so much higher than there (59.3%).

The honest result: relative momentum lands within a hair of the original — CAGR +39.9% vs. +40.6%, identical -35.1% max drawdown to one decimal place. pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Subtracting the SAME benchmark return from every stock that day is mathematically a shared, constant shift — it cannot, by itself, reorder which stock has the higher or lower raw return. The only reason relative momentum picks a DIFFERENT top 10 at all is that this shift happens before dividing by each stock's OWN volatility, which differs stock to stock: a low-volatility stock's score moves more (in ratio terms) from the same absolute shift than a high-volatility stock's does. That's a real effect, but a second-order one — which is exactly why 92.2% of picks stay the same, versus only 59.3% for report 33's skip-month variant, which changes the entire reference date every calculation is anchored to (a first-order effect, not a second-order one).

This is a useful negative result in its own right: it shows that "absolute vs. relative momentum" — a distinction that sounds conceptually important, and IS important in a genuinely divergent market (a crash where relative winners fall less, or a narrow rally where only some stocks participate) — doesn't necessarily produce a materially different portfolio in a market where midcap winners and the broad index have moved in the same general direction most of the time. A market regime with a sharper divergence between NIFTY 50 and midcap leadership (a narrow large-cap-only rally, for instance) would very plausibly separate these two formulas much more than this 18-year window happened to.

paragraphs: Unlike most other variants tested in this comparison series, front-loading recent momentum doesn't just move CAGR and drawdown in the same direction — it trades one for the other. panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.

A slow-moving average exits late into declines (giving back more before the filter reacts) and re-enters late into recoveries (missing more of the bounce), and in this specific 18-year path that combination cost both CAGR and drawdown protection relative to 200-day. This is a genuine finding about THIS historical window, not a general law that "wider is worse" — a different window could rank these four spans differently.

panels.heading: Why "wait for confirmation" isn't a free whipsaw fix

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: A confirmation delay works by definition: it ignores single-day or short-lived crossings of the EMA, so it only acts on moves that persist. That's exactly why re-entries fall so sharply (69 → 15 from 1-day to 10-day). The problem is that a REAL trend change also starts as a single day that has to persist before it's "confirmed" — so every extra day of confirmation is also an extra day of being on the wrong side of a genuine move, both entering AND exiting. Over 18 years, those extra wrong-side days added up to more lost CAGR than the avoided whipsaws saved, which is the honest reason the immediate 1-day switch — the version this project already tested in report 42 — comes out ahead of every slower alternative tried here.

This does NOT mean confirmation delays are a bad idea in general — a different EMA span, a different confirmation window, or a different market history could rank these differently, and a real trader who cares specifically about NOT paying commissions on 69 round-trips might still prefer a slower, cheaper-to-run variant even at this CAGR cost. What this report shows is that "add a confirmation delay" is a REAL trade-off to be made deliberately, not a strictly-better refinement of report 42's filter.

51.subtitle: Every Midcap150 Momentum 10 report so far has split each rebalance equally across the top 10 picks. The CAGR cost comes from the fact that in a momentum strategy, the highest-momentum names are often also the most volatile ones — down-weighting them because they're "shaky" also down-weights some of the strategy's own best performers.

panels.heading: Why down-weighting "shaky" names costs return here

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: A momentum strategy's whole premise is that stocks with strong recent price moves keep moving — and the stocks with the STRONGEST recent moves are frequently also the most volatile ones (rapid price appreciation and high volatility tend to travel together). Inverse-vol weighting is, in effect, a bet AGAINST the strategy's own strongest signals: it systematically shifts capital away from the very names the momentum score ranked highest by conviction (though not necessarily highest by SCORE, since the score itself already divides by volatility once) toward the calmer, more middling picks in the top 10.

The drawdown improvement is real but small — about a point — because the vol-based reweighting only shifts capital WITHIN an already-selected top 10; it can't do anything about a broad market crash that takes every stock in the portfolio down together (which is what actually drives most of this strategy's largest drawdowns). Report 42's 200-EMA regime filter, which sidesteps entire market downturns rather than reweighting within them, achieves a much bigger drawdown cut for a comparable CAGR cost.

panels.heading: Why breadth confirmation didn't add much here

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Breadth confirmation is a real, commonly-used idea in technical analysis — the logic is that a "healthy" market advance should be broad, not just a few large names pulling the index up while everything else lags, and a market where the index looks fine but breadth is deteriorating underneath is sometimes flagged as an early warning sign. The 90% threshold's slightly WORSE result (more re-entries for no better CAGR or drawdown) is itself instructive: a very strict breadth requirement doesn't wait for a genuinely different signal, it just makes the SAME underlying NIFTY-50 signal jumpier, since requiring near-unanimous participation is itself sensitive to whichever single stock happens to be right at its own 200-EMA on a given day. 58.title: Midcap150 Momentum 10 — Per-Stock Trailing Stop vs. Report 27's Fixed Stop
58.subtitle: Report 27 tested a FIXED stop-loss (15% and 30% below each position's own ENTRY price, never moving). This report tests the same two thresholds measured off each position's own PEAK price since entry instead — a trailing stop that ratchets UP as a winning position's peak rises, cutting individual losers without needing report 42-57's portfolio-wide regime switch at all. It stopped out 90.0% of every position ever held, at an AVERAGE return of +2.4% — often a small gain, not a loss, because the stop was simply too tight to survive ordinary price noise.

At 30%, the picture flips: trailing BEATS fixed on drawdown — -32.1% (fixed) improves to -29.4% (trailing) — for a modest CAGR cost, +35.0% to +31.3%. A WIDE trailing stop genuinely locks in gains on winners without over-triggering; a TIGHT one just adds noise-driven churn.

panels.heading: Why "trailing" isn't automatically "better"

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: A fixed stop is anchored to the ENTRY price for the whole holding period — a stock that rallies 40% then pulls back 15% from its peak is nowhere near a 15%-off-entry fixed stop (it's still up ~19% from entry), so it survives. A TRAILING stop has no such cushion: the moment that same stock's peak rises, the stop level rises right along with it, so a routine 15% pullback from ANY new high — completely normal for a volatile midcap stock, several times a year even during a genuine uptrend — triggers an exit. That's exactly why 90.0% of every position held was stopped out at 15% trailing, at a barely-positive average return: the stop was firing on ordinary noise, not on actual reversals.

A wide trailing stop (30%) avoids that failure mode — normal volatility rarely swings 30% from a recent peak within a 6-month window, so it mostly triggers on genuine, sustained reversals, which is exactly the scenario where locking in a rising floor pays off. The lesson generalizes beyond stop-losses: any rule that reacts to a MOVING reference point (a trailing peak, a moving average, a recent high) needs to be set wide enough to filter out routine noise, or it ends up reacting to volatility itself rather than to the trend it was meant to protect against — the same lesson report 46 found for EMA span and report 47 found for confirmation delay.

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: A 50-day EMA is much choppier than a 200-day one — it crosses back and forth across the price far more often, which is exactly why it's faster to react in the first place. 65.title: Midcap150 Momentum 10 — Volatility-Scaled (Smooth) Exposure
65.subtitle: Reports 42-64's regime filter flips 100%/0% the instant NIFTY 50 crosses its 200-day EMA. This report replaces the hard switch with a CONTINUOUS ramp: exposure scales linearly from 100% (at or above the EMA) down to 0% (a band_pct below it), removing the whipsaw problem at its root rather than tuning around it — there is no discrete state here at all, so there is nothing to "re-enter" or "confirm." Three band widths tested (10%/15%/20%) against the original and report 42's binary filter, all on the identical window.

paragraphs: Every band tested gives a HIGHER CAGR than the binary filter — +38.5% (binary) vs. +39.5% (10% band), +39.8% (15%), and +40.0% (20%) — while still cutting drawdown meaningfully versus no filter at all (-35.1%): -26.1%, -27.5%, and -28.3% respectively.

panels.heading: Why removing the whipsaw at its root pays off

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: The binary filter's own honesty notes (reports 42, 46, 47) repeatedly found that its biggest hidden cost is 69 whipsaw round-trips — full sells and full buys triggered by ordinary volatility near the 200-EMA, all charged nothing in this frictionless model but expensive in reality. A smooth ramp has NO discrete flip to whipsaw on: a day where price wobbles slightly above and below the EMA just nudges exposure a few percentage points, rather than triggering a full round-trip. Removing that specific cost is exactly why the smooth version's CAGR comes out ahead of the binary filter's at every band width tested, even though the binary filter still protects drawdown more deeply (it goes all the way to 0% exposure at the depth of a real crash, which the smooth version with a narrow band width only approaches asymptotically).

This IS still a genuinely different mechanism worth weighing, not a strict improvement: the 3.3% of days at fully zero exposure under the tightest (10%) band shows it still fully de-risks during the depths of a real crash, just via a smoother path in and out rather than a single hard switch.

81.title: Midcap150 Momentum 10 — Averaging Down Within the Holding Period
81.subtitle: Same top-10 momentum picks, same June/December rebalance, ONE continuous compounding portfolio — but instead of buying once and holding untouched, each stock's peak price since entry is tracked daily; the first time it falls 15% below that peak, an equal-sized top-up is bought, and if it falls 30% below peak, a second equal top-up follows. No new external money is used — every averaging buy is funded by trimming the OTHER 9 holdings proportionally, so the whole portfolio still compounds forward through every rebalance exactly like every other report here, and both variants get a single, directly comparable CAGR.

pills.text: averaging is basically a wash on CAGR, and makes the drawdown WORSE, not better

paragraphs: CAGR barely moves: +40.6% without averaging vs. +40.6% with it — a difference of 0.03 percentage points, functionally noise over 18 years. Max drawdown, though, gets meaningfully WORSE: -35.1% without averaging vs. -37.2% with it.

The mechanism is exactly what you'd expect once you look at where the money for each top-up actually comes from: since no new cash enters this portfolio, buying more of a stock that's already down 15-30% means SELLING a slice of the other 9 holdings — on average, the stocks that are doing BETTER — to fund it. That's selling strength to buy weakness, concentrating more of the portfolio into the position that's currently struggling, right when it's struggling. It roughly breaks even on return and makes the worst days worse.

paragraphs: The 15%-from-peak trigger fired 256 times (71.1% of all stock-periods) — a momentum pick pulling back 15% from its own peak-since-entry within a single 6-month window is common, not rare, for these volatile midcap names. The deeper 30% trigger fired 66 times (18.3%) — a real minority of positions, but still frequent enough to matter for how much gets trimmed from the winners.

panels.heading: Why "sell winners to buy the loser" roughly breaks even, but hurts on the worst days

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: This project's momentum formula tends to pick stocks BECAUSE they've already risen a lot — that's the entire selection criterion. A pick that then falls 15% from its post-purchase peak was, in this dataset, more often a pause within a continuing uptrend than the start of a real breakdown (256 triggers out of 360 positions is a LOT) — which is exactly why the CAGR effect nets out close to zero: money moved OUT of winners that mostly kept winning, and INTO a "loser" that mostly recovered anyway. Two roughly-offsetting costs, not a free lunch and not a disaster.

The drawdown cost is less forgiving: on the genuinely bad stretches — the ones that actually drive the portfolio's WORST days — concentrating more capital into the stock that's falling, funded by trimming the ones holding up better, is precisely the wrong trade at precisely the wrong moment. That's why max drawdown gets worse (-35.1% → -37.2%) even though the average outcome (CAGR) barely changes — the cost of averaging down shows up disproportionately in the tail, not in the typical case.

82.title: Midcap150 Momentum 10 — Averaging With Wider Triggers (25%/40%)
82.subtitle: Report 81's compounding-with-averaging design (top-up funded by trimming the OTHER 9 holdings, one continuous portfolio, single CAGR) found 15%/30% averaging was roughly a CAGR wash but made drawdown meaningfully worse — because most 15% pullbacks in this dataset were pauses within a continuing uptrend, not real breakdowns, so trimming winners to fund the top-up mostly cost something for nothing. This report widens the triggers to 25% and 40% off peak-since-entry to see whether firing less often, on more genuine dips, changes that trade-off.

pills.text: wider triggers flip the result — CAGR improves, and the drawdown cost shrinks

paragraphs: At 25%/40%, CAGR actually goes UP to +42.1% — better than both the no-averaging baseline (+40.6%) AND the tighter 15%/30% version (+40.6%). Drawdown is still slightly worse than no averaging (-36.0% vs. -35.1%), but meaningfully better than 15%/30%'s -37.2%.

The mechanism lines up with report 81's own explanation: the 25%-from-peak trigger fired on only 109 of 360 stock-periods (30.3%), less than half as often as 15%'s 256 (71.1%). Firing less often means trimming the OTHER 9 (better-performing, on average) holdings less often too — less of the "sell strength to buy weakness" drag that made 15%/30% a net negative on the worst days.

panels.heading: Why being more selective about WHICH dips to buy paid off

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Report 81's core finding still applies: this formula picks stocks BECAUSE they've already risen a lot, and a pullback from a post-purchase peak is, more often than not, a pause rather than a breakdown. The 15% trigger fires on 71% of positions — it's reacting to completely normal, routine volatility for these names, and every one of those top-ups costs a real trim from the other 9 holdings. The 25% trigger fires on only 30% of positions — rare enough that when it DOES fire, it's more likely catching something genuinely unusual, worth averaging into.

This doesn't mean wider is always better — push the trigger too wide (say, 60%/80%) and it would almost never fire, converging back toward the plain no-averaging baseline by construction. Somewhere between "fires on routine noise" (15%/30%) and "essentially never fires" there's a width where averaging has the best chance of adding value, and this result suggests 25%/40% sits closer to that zone than 15%/30% does — not proof it's the optimal width, just evidence the direction of the adjustment mattered.

83.title: Midcap150 Momentum 10 — Pyramiding Up Instead of Averaging Down
83.subtitle: Reports 81/82 tested buying MORE of a stock as it falls (15-40% below its own peak-since-entry). This report reverses the idea: buy more of a stock as it RISES — the first time it closes 20% above its own buy price, top up with an amount equal to the original allocation; the first time it closes 40% above buy price, a second equal top-up follows. Same funding mechanism as 81/82 (trim the other 9 holdings proportionally, no new external capital, one continuous compounding portfolio, single CAGR) — the only thing that changes is the direction of the trigger.

pills.text: buying more of a winner while it keeps winning beats buying more of a loser hoping it recovers

paragraphs: Pyramiding up lifts CAGR from +40.6% to +41.6% — a real, if modest, improvement — for only a small drawdown cost: -35.1% without it vs. -35.6% with it. That's a meaningfully BETTER trade-off than either down-side design tested in reports 81/82 — report 81's 15%/30% averaging-down was a CAGR wash with a bigger drawdown cost (-37.2%), and report 82's wider 25%/40% down-trigger beat this on CAGR (+42.1%) but at a deeper drawdown (-36.0%) than pyramiding up's -35.6%.

The mechanism makes sense given what this formula actually selects for: these are picks chosen BECAUSE they already rose a lot over the past 6-12 months. Buying more as that same trend continues is betting WITH the selection criterion; buying more as it reverses is betting AGAINST it. Pyramiding up is the more momentum-consistent of the two ideas, and it performs like it.

paragraphs: Every top-up in this report, like reports 81/82, is funded by trimming the OTHER 9 holdings — there's no free lunch, capital always comes from somewhere. 87.subtitle: Report 85 could only compare the six semi-annual rebalance calendars one at a time — picking a winner meant guessing in advance which two months would turn out best. This report asks what happens if you don't pick: split capital equally (1/6 each) across ALL SIX calendars — June/December, July/January, August/February, September/March, October/April, November/May — as six independently-compounding sleeves of the same 200-day EMA + gold design, then combine them into one blended portfolio.

pills.text: the blend beats report 48's own June/December on CAGR, while staying close to its drawdown

paragraphs: The blended portfolio returns +43.2% CAGR with a -24.0% drawdown — better CAGR than report 48's own June/December calendar (+42.7%), for only -0.6 percentage points more drawdown (-23.4%). It lands almost exactly in the MIDDLE of the six individual calendars' CAGR range (+41.4% to +44.7%) — expected for an equal-weight average — but its drawdown is the SECOND-BEST of all seven options shown here (six single calendars plus the blend), only just behind June/December's own.

The practical value: you never had to know in advance that June/December would turn out to have the best drawdown, or that July/January would have the best CAGR. Blending all six gets most of the benefit of picking well, without having to actually guess — a real diversification effect, not a coincidence of these particular six numbers.

panels.heading: Why blending shallows the drawdown without giving up CAGR

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Each calendar's own worst drawdown happens on ITS OWN specific rebalance dates — whichever ten stocks a given calendar happened to be holding right as a bad stretch hit. Since the six calendars' rebalance dates are spread roughly a month apart from each other, they're rarely all badly positioned on the exact same day. Blending means the portfolio's WORST day is an average across six sleeves that don't all bottom out simultaneously — some calendars will have already refreshed into fresher picks by the time others are still holding stale ones, smoothing the combined trough shallower than most of the individual lines.

CAGR, being an average of six numbers that are all comfortably positive and fairly close together (+41.4% to +44.7%), simply lands near the middle — averaging doesn't cost much on the upside because none of the six individual calendars is dramatically better or worse than the others to begin with. The combination of "averages out to close to the middle on CAGR" and "smooths out the specific worst day on drawdown" is what makes blending land favorably here — a portfolio that never has to bet everything on one specific two-month pair.

89.title: Midcap150 Momentum 10 — Report 48 With 0.1% Slippage
89.subtitle: Report 48's exact design — the 200-day EMA regime filter, gold instead of cash — with a real trading cost applied for the first time: every buy fills 0.1% ABOVE the modeled price, every sell fills 0.1% BELOW it. Every transition in this design (a regime exit, a regime re-entry, or the scheduled semi-annual refresh) is really a two-leg trade — sell whatever's currently held, buy whatever it's moving into — so slippage is charged on BOTH legs, every time. Zero transaction costs has been a disclosed simplification in every report here so far, including report 48 itself; this tests how much of the reported edge survives once a real cost is actually charged.

paragraphs: CAGR drops from +43.3% to +40.6% — a real, meaningful cost, not a rounding error. Max drawdown gets WORSE too, not just CAGR: -23.4% frictionless vs. -25.5% with slippage — every regime switch INTO gold during a crash now sells stocks at a worse price and buys gold at a worse price too, right when the strategy can least afford it.

The design still comfortably beats NIFTY 50 (+12.5%) even after this cost — but 0.1% slippage, a small-sounding number, adds up over 95 separate buy/sell events across 18 years into a genuinely large compounding drag. This is the single biggest gap between a "backtest number" and a "number you could actually expect to live with" that this project has shown for report 48 so far.

•Exit rank N: a holder is sold at a review only when its fit rank falls below N of the ~150 eligible names; the freed slot is refilled with the best-ranked non-held name.
•Daily-breach mode: the same rank check runs at every close — a holder is sold THAT day (0.1% cost) and the slot waits in cash until the next Jun/Dec review.
•Entry rank K: new buys may only come from the top K ranks; an open slot waits in cash until a name reaches the top K — never redistributed to other slots.
•Sector caps use Yahoo Finance's present-day sector for each NIFTY 500 name (sectors_raw.json, fetched once for report 18) applied backwards; a name without a sector is uncapped.
•Whole units: share quantities are floored to integers on every buy and the leftover rupee amount stays in cash.
•Friction variants add slippage on top of the base 0.1% cost — 0.3% and 0.5% per side total, the honest stress test for a 2-rebalance-a-year system.
•Health, halves and the tax layer are computed per variant with the same ms_port code report 93 uses; after-tax curves follow report 93's conventions (indicative, not advice).

paragraphs: The winners stack into a modest, honest improvement. keep-if 6m > 0 + exit rank 30 — 'max stack A' — gives 40.0% CAGR at -24.0% max drawdown and health 70/100, against the hero's 39.5% / -25.4% / 60. The honesty battery: whole units 39.8% / -23.9%; 0.5%/side friction still 31.1%; both-halves robustness passes on every row; and all six rebalance calendars — the same six report 92 tested — land between 38.2% and 40.1% for both stacks, so the result is not a June/December artifact (though Jun/Dec does happen to be the best of the six — a 1.8pp date-luck spread worth knowing about).

The money plan on top — SIP ₹25k/month with a 10%/yr step-up plus ₹25k dip top-ups — turns ₹1.39 Cr of contributions into ₹41.4 Cr at the window's end (30×), the fullest version of this strategy these labs produced.

99.title: Timing Audit — the Gold-Strength Guard's +11.5pp That Wasn't
99.subtitle: Reports 91/92 introduced a guard on report 48's hedge leg: during a risk-off period, hold gold only while gold's own ~6-month return beats NIFTY's and is positive — else sit in flat cash. The first release claimed the guard added 11.5–11.9 points of CAGR on every rebalance calendar and cut drawdown to −20.0%. This report recomputes the published logic exactly as it shipped, side by side with the corrected logic, on one identical window, and accounts for every rupee of the difference.

pills.text: same code, two timings: +11.86pp of CAGR collapses to +0.07pp

paragraphs: The published guard showed CAGR rising from +42.0% to +53.9% — a terminal multiple of 4.16× report 48. Corrected, the same guard produces +42.1% — 1.01×. Roughly all of the difference came from two classes of days where the published code used information it could not have had live: flip-off days (whose realized return in report 48 is still stocks — the switch executes at that day's close) and same-day exit checks (flat cash applied to the very close that tripped the check).

What survives is honest and small: +42.1% vs +42.0% (+0.07pp), with max drawdown improving +0.79pp (-23.4% → -22.6%). Reports 91 and 92 now publish these corrected numbers; this report is the audit trail.

One more page carried the same phantom: the earlier findings-round release of this idea (the "Gold-Strength Guard Before Switching to Gold" finding, f10) published the identical double-digit gains across Midcap150, Smallcap250 and NIFTY100, on the same flawed day-level masks. It has been regenerated with this fix — its Midcap150 top-10 "both checks" variant now reads 42.08% CAGR / −22.63% drawdown (report 48's own, same window: 42.01% / −23.42%), versus the 54.80% / −19.95% it published at its older data vintage — and across all nine universe/size variants the honest effect runs −0.2 to +0.9pp of CAGR with drawdown between 0.8pp better and 1.4pp worse.

A second findings page, "Wild Combinations on Report 48" (f3), carried the same class of phantom: its two gold-trend-filter variants (G/H) were that batch's headline at 53.2% / 53.5% CAGR, having read gold's own trend with each day's close and substituted the same day's return on the very close that tripped the check. Corrected to the prior-close convention they land at 43.21% / −22.6% and 42.90% / −23.2% (report 48's own, same window: 42.01% / −23.42%) — real but small: +1.2pp and +0.9pp of CAGR with drawdowns 0.2–0.8pp shallower. The page and its results file have been regenerated.

panels.heading: The arithmetic — every rupee accounted for

pills.text: reconciliation

paragraphs: The two mechanisms touch disjoint sets of days, so their effects multiply: 1.90× (zeroing same-day-detected fail days — the "small" half) × 2.19× (resubstituting boundary and transition days with gold) = 4.16× — exactly the published terminal multiple. With both corrected, the guard's multiple over report 48 is 1.01×. Over a 2009-01-02–2026-10-15 window, a 4.16× head start compounds to the +11.86pp of CAGR that was published; 1.01× compounds to +0.07pp.

panels.heading: Limitations & the general lesson

pills.text: read before trusting any number above

list_items:
The corrected guard itself is not "proven good": +0.07pp of CAGR is inside
        any plausible cost band, and −0.79pp of drawdown is a trim, not a transformation. Reports
        91/92 now present it that way.

The rule this audit enforces project-wide: strategies that act at a day's close must be evaluated on
        PRIOR-close information — a day's realized return belongs to the state decided at the previous close. Any day-level
        substitution (hedge swaps, exit checks, recovery dodges) is exactly where this class of bug hides, and aggregate metrics
        cannot see it — crash-day tables are the only way.

Zero transaction costs throughout, matching reports 91/92's own convention; the guard adds few extra
        switch events (~247 flat days across 21-odd regime blocks), so costs do not change the
        audit's conclusions about the artifact.

Same reconstruction caveats as everywhere in this project: today's fixed Midcap150 constituent list
        applied retroactively (survivorship bias), equal weighting, unadjusted prices, no dividends.
